Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Go first with a light example of your own, and never ask a student to speak for a group. Say plainly that switching to stay safe from bias is on the people doing the treating.

Every student in the room

Language, race, money, faith, neurodivergence and LGBTQ+ identity all come up here; let students choose what they share, and say plainly that switching to stay safe from bias is on the people doing the treating.

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Go first with your own example. Expect laughs, slang, a home language, a nickname only family uses. Point out that everyone just showed a skill: reading a room and adjusting.

Slide 3 · Notes

Private tally marks on the card. Don’t collect cards and don’t ask anyone to share which. Money often gets the quietest marks; if it fits your group, name it plainly.

Slide 4 · Notes

Hands up, then the answer. Nobody says which marks they made.

Slide 5 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 6 · Notes

Road games aren’t bad, and good teams win them. A team that only plays away games gets worn down.

Slide 7 · Notes

Two minutes. Collect a few answers on the board. If a student says they don’t have one, note it gently and check in afterward.

Slide 8 · Notes

Write a few on the board. Then: what the research says.

Slide 9 · Notes

Racial code switching can make people seem more professional to others, and it also costs effort. Say plainly: if someone switches because they’re treated differently for who they are, that unfairness is on the people doing the treating.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

Point out that being called fake or told “you’ve changed” adds its own stress.

Slide 12 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 13 · Notes

Money switches in a lot of ways: trips, phones, clothes, who drives. Keep it about what a friend can do.

Slide 14 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 15 · Notes

Private writing; no sharing required. Share the take-home link. If switching wears a student out most days, or someone treats them differently for who they are, a counselor is a good person to talk to.

Slide 16 · Notes

Coming out is the student’s call. Switching isn’t fake, and it isn’t wrong. Watch for students carrying a lot.

Share the take-home link. It lists who to talk to.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can describe code switching as a normal skill, name what it can protect and what it can cost, and identify one place where they get to be all the way themselves. Nobody is asked to name their race, culture, religion, gender, sexuality or disability, or to share what they switch.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • A board or chart paper
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minThree rooms: how do you talk in each?
  2. 3 minWhat people switch (private tally), hands up
  3. 2 minHome games and away games
  4. 3 minWhat makes a home game? Turn and talk, share out
  5. 3 minThe research guess
  6. 4 minTwo moments: Jesse, Ava
  7. 2 minName one home game, close

Short on time (10-minute check-in)

Three rooms, the private tally, home and away games, and one home game.

Before you teach
Go first, lightly.

Share a low-stakes example of your own: how you talk on the phone with your grandmother versus a parent-teacher conference, or the voice you use with a coach. It shows everyone switches, including adults, and keeps the room from turning toward any one student.

Never ask a student to speak for a group.

Don't call on the one student of a background to explain what switching is like for "their" community. Students choose what they share, and passing is always fine.

Switching isn't fake, and it isn't wrong.

Avoid framing one way of talking as "proper" and another as "slang." Every dialect and home language has its own rules. Linguists call Black English, for example, a full language variety with consistent grammar.

Unfairness is real. Name it without a lecture.

Some students switch to stay safe from bias. Say plainly that's on the people treating them differently, not on them. You don't need to resolve it in 20 minutes.

Coming out is the student's call.

Gender and sexuality come up on the student page as things people sometimes hide. Never guess, never out anyone, and don't ask students to say whether this applies to them.

Money switches too, in a lot of ways.

At an independent school, money comes up constantly: trips over break, phones and clothes, eating out, camps, birthday plans, who drives and who takes the bus, who works after school or cares for siblings, who's on financial aid. In your own check-ins, ask "What was one good part of your break?" rather than "Where did you go?", keep plans that cost money optional, and never ask students to compare.

Watch for students carrying a lot.

A student who says they can't be themselves anywhere, or who describes being targeted for who they are, is worth a quiet check-in after advisory and a same-day note to a counselor.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Language at home.

Some students speak another language at home, translate for parents, or are told they're losing their home language. Treat all of it as an asset, not a gap.

Race and ethnicity.

Research on racial code switching mostly involves Black students and adults, and it applies to many others too. Keep examples broad and let students connect them to their own lives if they want.

Neurodivergence.

Autistic students and students with ADHD often describe "masking": hiding traits to fit in, which can be exhausting. The home games idea fits them too.

LGBTQ+ students.

Some students switch how they show their gender or who they like, depending on who's around. Safety comes first; the lesson never asks anyone to be more out than they choose.

Money and class.

Students switch around money: what they say they did over break, where they live, what they can afford, whether they're on financial aid. Some students spend breaks working or caring for siblings. Keep examples free of brand names and trips, and treat family responsibilities as strengths.

Faith.

Some students tone down their faith at school, or tone down school at home. Both are worth respecting.

What the research says

Linguists have studied code switching for decades and describe it as a skilled, rule-governed way people use language to signal identity and fit a setting.

Gumperz, Discourse Strategies, 1982

A meta-analysis of 83 studies (more than 23,000 people) found that being bicultural, holding two cultures rather than choosing one, was linked to better psychological and social adjustment.

Nguyen & Benet-Martínez, Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 2013

Black professionals who code switched were seen as more professional by others, which shows why people switch, and the researchers also describe its costs in effort and authenticity.

McCluney et al., Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 2021

Among Black college students, being accused of "acting White" was linked to their mental health, and the link depended on how they felt about their own racial identity.

Durkee & Williams, Journal of Black Psychology, 2015

In a national survey, 61% of employees said they hide or downplay some part of their identity at work, a pattern called covering.

Yoshino & Smith, Deloitte, 2013
